To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) glutamate receptor activation of the bipolar cells is mediated by a combination of AMPA, kainate and NMDA receptor subtypes, and the bipolar cells are regulated by GABAergic inhibition, (2) the mitral and the tufted cells are activated through glutamate receptors, including the kainate and the NMDA receptor types, and the mitral and tufed cells are regulated by reciprocal regulation through dendro-dendritic GABAergic synapses

the bipolar, mitra and tufted cell neurones are segregated into parallel ON and OF responses to light exposure, and are regulated through dendrodendrite synapses with their inhibitory granule cells, and that the segregation and regulation are achieved through the activation and inactivation of specific types of voltage-dependent ion channels and metabotropic glutamate receptors.

the bipolar cells segregate the visual input into parallel ON and Off responses to light exposure by means of the NMDA and GABAA receptor-mediated mechanisms, respectively, and that the mitral and the tufted cells discriminate the olfactory input by the dendrodendritic synaptic mechanisms, and undergo the synaptic regulation of olfactory recognition memory formation by the NMDA receptor-mediated mechanisms.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fundamental synaptic mechanisms underlying visual and olfactory information processing, and the modulation of the synaptic mechanisms involved in olfactory recognition memory.
the molecular mechanisms of synaptic transmission and synaptic plasticity in the visual and olfactory systems.
the synaptic operation and plasticity of the second-order neurons in the retina and olfactory bulbs, as well as with the synaptic mechanisms of the higher-order visual and olfactory neurons.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the synaptic mechanisms of the bipolar, and mitral and tuften cells, are essential to understand the basic synaptic operation of the brain.

the second-order neurone is the first level of sensory-information processing, and that the synaptic mechanism of the second-order cells is the fundamental mechanism of sensory-information processing.
the second-order neurone is the basic unit of the sensory-information processing system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the second-order neurone, as a central relay of the sensory system, plays a key role in the processing of information and in the modulation of the information processing, and the molecular mechanisms of these operations are now becoming clear.
the second-order neurone is an important site of the sensory information processing, where synaptic operation and regulation are crucial for the segregation and discrimination.

, at the molecular and synaptic level, second-order sensory neurones are capable of segregating sensory inputs into parallel ON- and OFF-responses, and of forming memory traces for olfactory-recognition.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the molecular mechanisms of synaptic plasticity are not restricted to the synapses of the first-order sensory neurones, and that synaptic plasticity is a general feature of all synapses in the central nervous system, including those of higher-order sensory neurones.
the second-order neurone, in addition to being the first relay of information, is a site where information is processed and regulated.

second-order sensory neurones are capable of processing sensory signals and regulating the information flow through the brain, and that these functions are mediated by the molecular mechanisms that regulate synaptic transmission.
